one_liner: Clang plugin plus runtime that re-optimises a C++ function at run time with some arguments fixed as constants; beats the generic AOT build.
what_it_does: A Clang pass embeds the LLVM bitcode of selected functions in the binary; at run time easy::jit(fn, args..., _1, _2) takes the known argument values plus std::placeholders and returns a callable (FunctionWrapper) with the remaining parameters, compiled for those values. easy::Cache<> memoises specialisations keyed on function and argument values, and options let you set the opt level or dump the generated IR. It is not a drop-in: you must build with clang and the EasyJitPass plugin, link EasyJitRuntime and the LLVM libraries, and the function's body must be visible (EASY_JIT_EXPOSE or -mllvm -easy-export regex).
how_it_is_fast: Runtime partial evaluation (value specialisation): known arguments are inlined as constants (InlineParameters pass), constant function pointers are devirtualised (DevirtualizeConstant pass), then the standard LLVM -O2 pipeline runs, so loop bounds become constants, small loops fully unroll and indirect calls such as a qsort comparator get inlined. Code is generated by the legacy LLVM ExecutionEngine (MCJIT, CodeGenOpt::Aggressive) with -mcpu set to the host CPU, so it can also use ISA extensions the AOT binary was not built for.
when_to_use: A hot generic kernel whose parameters (filter mask, sizes, strides, channel count, a callback pointer) are fixed for a long run but only known at run time, e.g. per video stream or per loaded config.
Callback-heavy C-style code (qsort-like comparators, function-pointer tables) where inlining the callback is the main win.
Research or prototyping of runtime specialisation on an LLVM 6 toolchain you can pin, where writing templates for every parameter combination is impractical.
Long-running loops that amortise compile cost: the blog cites break-even after about 2 convolution calls and 29 quicksort calls at size 1024.
when_not_to_use: Any toolchain newer than LLVM/Clang 6.0: CMake requires find_package(LLVM 6.0), issue #42 (move to LLVM 7) and #51 (link errors on LLVM 14.0.6, port only in a third-party fork) are open, and the project is abandoned since 2021-05-15.
GCC or MSVC builds: the method needs the Clang plugin at compile time and the LLVM JIT libraries at run time.

Short-lived or latency-sensitive calls: every new argument combination pays a full LLVM -O2 plus codegen compile (the pipeline is populated twice in Optimize()), and that cost is excluded from the quoted speedups.
When the parameter set is small and known at build time: templates or constexpr specialisation give the same code without a JIT or a large LLVM runtime dependency.
Production use: open issues report every example failing with an InlineParameters assertion (#43) and 'Pass registered multiple times' crashes (#45), all unanswered.

integration.form: Clang pass plugin (EasyJitPass.so) plus a shared runtime library (EasyJitRuntime) and headers
integration.dependencies: LLVM 6.0 and clang 6.0 (development packages), Python lit for tests; optional OpenCV for examples and Google Benchmark for the benchmark
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 and aarch64 detected in CMake; other hosts not documented
integration.thread_safety: Not documented; easy::Cache is an unsynchronised std::unordered_map and the BitcodeTracker is a global static without locks, so concurrent jit or cache calls need external locking.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: the function body stays unchanged, but call sites must go through easy::jit or easy::Cache and the whole project must be built with clang plus the plugin

gotchas: Harness flaw: benchmark/CMakeLists.txt adds only '-Xclang -disable-O0-optnone' and the plugin to CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS and sets no optimisation level, and the README build line passes no CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE, so a build that follows the README compiles the AOT baseline (kernel, Qsort) at -O0 for generic x86-64 while the JIT side always runs the LLVM -O2 pipeline with CodeGenOpt::Aggressive and -mcpu=host; the blog's 4.5x and 2x do not state which build was timed, and a WebSearch summary cites about 8x against an -O2 static build (source not identified).

Harness flaws in benchmark/benchmark.cpp: BM_convolve allocates (n-3)^2 ints but writes index i*(n-2)+j up to (n-4)(n-1), out of bounds for every n of 5 or more; the image is all zeros; Qsort tests 'if (cmp(...))' instead of '< 0', so with distinct keys every element moves left, recursion depth is n and the timed work is an O(n^2) chain of comparator calls that does not sort; JIT compile time is excluded from the timed loop.
The catalogue record says LLVM ORC; the runtime (runtime/Function.cpp) actually uses the legacy llvm::ExecutionEngine (EngineBuilder, EngineKind::JIT), not ORC.
Functions not deduced automatically must be exported with EASY_JIT_EXPOSE or -mllvm -easy-export, otherwise easy::jit throws BitcodeNotRegistered at run time.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over AsmJit or sljit when you want to specialise existing C++ source rather than emit machine code by hand, and over RapidUDF when the code to speed up is a C++ function, not an expression string; TPDE solves compile latency of LLVM back-ends and is complementary, not an alternative.
verified_claims_summary: First-party Quarkslab blog (EuroLLVM/FOSDEM 2018 era, read only as a search snippet): the specialised convolution kernel ran about 4.5x and the comparator-inlined quicksort about 2x faster than the same functions compiled ahead of time, sizes 16 to 1024, compile time excluded; no CPU, compiler flags or build type are given, and the repo harness behind these numbers has the out-of-bounds write, non-sorting comparator test and unset -O level described under gotchas.
status_note: Abandoned since 2021-05-15 and pinned to LLVM/Clang 6.0 with crash reports unanswered; BSD-3-Clause, so usable as a reference design for runtime specialisation, but porting to a current LLVM (a third-party llvm-14.0.6 branch exists with link errors) is the price of using it.
